lessons.title: How bonding and structure explain properties
lessons.summary: Link the particle model and the four main structure types (ionic, small molecules, giant covalent and metallic) to melting points, conductivity and strength, so you can predict how a substance behaves from how it is bonded.
objectives: I can use the particle model to explain changes of state and use state symbols in equations.
I can explain why ionic compounds have high melting points and only conduct when molten or dissolved.
I can explain why small molecules have low melting points and do not conduct electricity.
I can explain the properties of polymers, giant covalent structures, metals and alloys in terms of their bonding.

activities.title: States of matter and the particle model
activities.content:
## Solids, liquids and gases

The **particle model** pictures every substance as tiny particles that are arranged and move differently in each state:

| State | Arrangement | Movement | Can it flow? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Solid | regular, touching | vibrate in fixed positions | no |
| Liquid | random, touching | slide past each other | yes |
| Gas | random, far apart | move fast in all directions | yes |

**Melting** and **boiling** need energy to overcome the forces holding particles together. The stronger those forces, the **higher the melting and boiling points**.

In equations we show the state with a **state symbol**: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) dissolved in water. So $NaCl(s)$ is solid salt but $NaCl(aq)$ is salty water.

The model is useful but simplified. It treats particles as solid, inelastic spheres with nothing between them, and it says nothing about the forces between particles, which is exactly what decides most properties. This lesson fills that gap.

question.text: Which state symbol shows that a substance is dissolved in water?
question.hint: The symbol comes from the Latin word for water.
question.explanation: (aq) stands for aqueous, meaning dissolved in water. (l) means a pure liquid.

options.feedback: (l) is a pure liquid, such as molten salt or pure water.

activities.title: Ionic compounds
activities.content:
## Giant ionic lattices

Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride and magnesium oxide are built as a **giant lattice**: a regular, repeating 3D arrangement of positive and negative ions held together by **strong electrostatic forces** acting in all directions. This is **ionic bonding**.

That structure explains their properties:

- **High melting and boiling points.** A lot of energy is needed to break the many strong bonds between oppositely charged ions. Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C.
- **Do not conduct electricity when solid.** The ions are locked in place and cannot move.
- **Conduct when molten or dissolved in water.** Now the ions are free to move and carry charge.

A common slip is to say "electrons flow" in a molten ionic compound. It is the **ions** that move, not electrons.

Magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻) melts at over 2800 °C, much higher than sodium chloride (Na⁺ and Cl⁻), because doubly charged ions attract each other more strongly.

activities.title: Worked example: explaining conductivity
activities.content:
**A student tests three samples of potassium bromide with a bulb and electrodes. Solid: bulb off. Molten: bulb on. Solution in water: bulb on. Explain the results.**

*Solid:* potassium bromide is a giant ionic lattice. The K⁺ and Br⁻ ions are held firmly in fixed positions by strong electrostatic attraction, so no charged particles can move and no current flows.

*Molten:* the heat has broken the lattice apart. Ions are now free to move towards the electrodes, so charge is carried through the liquid.

*Solution:* dissolving separates the ions, which spread through the water and can move freely. Again, the ions carry the current.

Notice the structure of the answer: name the particles, say whether they can move, link movement to conduction.

question.text: Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
question.hint: What type of force holds the ions together, and how many bonds must be broken?
question.explanation: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these many strong forces.

markScheme.criterion: Strong electrostatic forces / strong ionic bonds between oppositely charged ions
A lot of energy is needed to break / overcome them

activities.title: Small molecules
activities.content:
## Simple molecular substances

Water, carbon dioxide, methane, oxygen and chlorine are all made of **small molecules**: a few atoms joined by **covalent bonds**.

Here is the idea students most often get wrong. Inside a molecule the covalent bonds are **strong**. But *between* molecules there are only **weak intermolecular forces**. When you melt or boil a molecular substance you break the **weak forces between molecules**, not the covalent bonds. That is why:

- Small molecules have **low melting and boiling points**; many are gases or liquids at room temperature.
- **Larger molecules** have **stronger intermolecular forces**, so bigger molecules have higher melting and boiling points. Chlorine (Cl₂) is a gas, bromine (Br₂) a liquid and iodine (I₂) a solid.
- They **do not conduct electricity**. Molecules have no overall charge and there are no free electrons or ions.

An exam answer that says "the covalent bonds are weak so it has a low boiling point" scores zero. Always say **weak forces between molecules**.

question.text: True or false: when water boils, the covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken.
question.hint: What escapes as steam: separate atoms or whole H₂O molecules?
question.explanation: False. Boiling overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between water molecules. The molecules stay intact; the O–H covalent bonds are not broken.

activities.title: Polymers and giant covalent structures
activities.content:
## Very large covalent structures

**Polymers** are very long molecules made of thousands of repeating units joined by covalent bonds, such as poly(ethene). Because the molecules are so long, the **intermolecular forces between chains are relatively strong**, so polymers are **solids at room temperature**. They still do not conduct electricity, and they soften and melt at fairly modest temperatures because the chains only need to slide apart, not break.

**Giant covalent structures** go one step further: every atom is covalently bonded to its neighbours in an enormous network. Examples are **diamond**, **graphite** and **silicon dioxide** (silica, the main substance in sand).

- **Very high melting points.** Melting means breaking millions of strong covalent bonds, which needs huge amounts of energy.
- Usually **hard** (diamond) and **do not conduct** electricity (graphite is the exception because of its delocalised electrons; you will meet it in the next sub-topic).

The key distinction: a polymer is a large *molecule* held to other molecules by intermolecular forces; a giant covalent structure is one continuous network with no separate molecules at all.

question.text: Match each substance to the type of structure it has.
question.hint: Ask: is it made of ions, small molecules, a huge network of atoms, or metal atoms?
question.explanation: Magnesium oxide is ionic; methane is a small molecule; silicon dioxide is a giant covalent network; copper is a metal with a giant metallic lattice.

activities.title: Metals and alloys
activities.content:
## Metallic structures

A metal is a **giant structure of atoms arranged in regular layers**, with the outer electrons **delocalised** (free to move through the whole structure). The attraction between the positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons is **metallic bonding**, and it is strong.

- **High melting points**: lots of energy is needed to break the strong metallic bonds.
- **Good conductors of electricity and heat**: the delocalised electrons can move and carry charge or thermal energy.
- **Malleable**: the layers of atoms can **slide over each other** without the bonding breaking, so metals can be bent and hammered into shape.

Pure metals are often *too* soft. An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with small amounts of other elements. The added atoms are a **different size**, which **distorts the regular layers** so they can no longer slide easily. That is why alloys such as brass (copper + zinc) and steel (iron + carbon) are **harder** than the pure metals.

A good sketch: neat rows of same-sized circles for a pure metal; rows with a few bigger or smaller circles jammed in for an alloy.

activities.title: Worked example: pure metal versus alloy
activities.content:
**Why is 24-carat (pure) gold too soft for a wedding ring, while 18-carat gold (75% gold mixed with copper and silver) is hard enough?**

*Pure gold:* the atoms are all the same size and sit in perfectly regular layers. Under a force the layers **slide over one another** easily, so the ring bends and scratches.

*18-carat gold:* the copper and silver atoms are **different sizes** from gold atoms. They **disrupt the regular layers**, so the layers cannot slide as easily. The alloy resists bending and scratching, making it far more practical for jewellery worn every day.

Notice that the delocalised electrons are still there, so the alloy still conducts and is still shiny; the only property that changed is hardness.

question.text: Complete the explanation of why alloys are harder than pure metals.

metadata.blanksText: In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in regular ___ that can slide over each other. In an alloy, atoms of a different ___ distort the arrangement, so the layers cannot ___ as easily.

question.hint: Think about the drawing of a pure metal compared with an alloy.
question.explanation: Pure metals have regular layers that slide. Added atoms of a different size distort the layers so they cannot slide, making the alloy harder.

question.text:
The table shows some properties of two substances.

| Substance | Melting point (°C) | Conducts when solid? | Conducts when molten? |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 770 | no | yes |
| B | −23 | no | no |

(a) Identify the type of structure of substance A and explain the conductivity results. (3 marks)

(b) Identify the type of structure of substance B and explain its low melting point. (2 marks)
question.hint: Conducting only when molten is the signature of one structure type. A very low melting point with no conduction at all is the signature of another.
question.explanation: (a) A is a giant ionic lattice. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, so it does not conduct; when molten the ions are free to move and carry the charge. (b) B is made of small (simple) molecules. Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome to melt it, which needs little energy.

markScheme.criterion: A is ionic / a giant ionic lattice
In the solid, ions are fixed in position / cannot move so no conduction
When molten, ions are free to move and carry charge
B is a small / simple molecular substance
Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome, needing little energy

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Melting and boiling points depend on the **strength of the forces between particles**.
- **Ionic**: giant lattice, strong electrostatic forces, high melting point, conducts only when molten or dissolved (ions move).
- **Small molecules**: strong covalent bonds inside, **weak intermolecular forces** between, low melting points, no conduction; bigger molecules have higher boiling points.
- **Polymers**: very long molecules, solid at room temperature.
- **Giant covalent**: every atom bonded, very high melting points (diamond, graphite, silica).
- **Metals**: layers of ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; conduct, malleable. **Alloys** are harder because different-sized atoms stop layers sliding.

practiceQuestions.text: In which state are particles arranged randomly, touching each other and able to slide past one another?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is the state that can flow but has a fixed volume.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In a liquid the particles are close together but not in a regular pattern, and they can move past each other.

options.feedback: Gas particles are far apart, not touching.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: solid ionic compounds conduct electricity because their electrons are free to move.
practiceQuestions.hint: Are there any charged particles that can move in a solid ionic lattice?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because the ions are fixed in place. Even when molten it is ions, not electrons, that carry the charge.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these substances in order of increasing boiling point.
practiceQuestions.hint: For small molecules, bigger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces; giant structures are highest of all.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fluorine (F₂) and chlorine (Cl₂) are small molecules; chlorine is larger so has the higher boiling point. Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice with far stronger forces to overcome.

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are properties of metals explained by delocalised electrons? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Delocalised electrons carry things through the metal.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Delocalised electrons carry charge (electrical conduction) and thermal energy (heat conduction). Malleability is explained by layers sliding; high density is about mass and packing, not electrons.

options.feedback: Malleability is because layers of atoms slide over each other.

practiceQuestions.text: Bromine melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C. Over how many degrees Celsius is bromine a liquid?
practiceQuestions.hint: Subtract the melting point from the boiling point. Take care with the negative number.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about giant covalent structures.

metadata.blanksText: Diamond and silicon dioxide have very high melting points because many strong ___ bonds must be broken, which needs a large amount of ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: What kind of bond joins non-metal atoms?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The atoms are joined by covalent bonds throughout the structure; breaking them needs a great deal of energy.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why carbon dioxide does not conduct electricity in any state.
practiceQuestions.hint: What charged particles would be needed, and does CO₂ have any?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is made of neutral molecules. There are no ions and no delocalised electrons, so there are no charged particles free to move and carry a current.

markScheme.criterion: Made of molecules with no overall charge / no ions
No free / delocalised electrons to carry charge

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement correctly explains why poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature while ethene is a gas?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the size of the molecules.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Poly(ethene) molecules are very long, so the intermolecular forces between them are much stronger than between small ethene molecules. More energy is needed to separate them.

options.text: Poly(ethene) molecules are much larger, so the intermolecular forces are stronger
Poly(ethene) has ionic bonds but ethene does not
The covalent bonds in poly(ethene) are stronger than those in ethene
options.feedback: The C–C and C–H covalent bonds are similar; the difference is in forces between molecules.

options.text: Poly(ethene) is a giant covalent structure

practiceQuestions.text:
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. It is used for door handles because it is harder than pure copper.

(a) Describe the structure of a pure metal. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why brass is harder than pure copper. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Draw the two structures in your head: regular layers versus layers with odd-sized atoms mixed in.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) A pure metal is a giant structure of atoms (positive ions) arranged in regular layers, with delocalised electrons between them. (b) Zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms, so they distort the layers. The layers can no longer slide over each other easily, making brass harder.

markScheme.criterion: Atoms / positive ions arranged in regular layers
Delocalised electrons / sea of electrons between the ions
Zinc atoms are a different size and distort / disrupt the layers
So the layers cannot slide over each other as easily

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is a limitation of the simple particle model?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what the little circles in the diagrams leave out.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The simple model shows particles as solid spheres with nothing between them and ignores the forces between particles, which actually decide melting and boiling points.

options.text: It does not show the forces between particles
It cannot explain why liquids flow

practiceQuestions.text: Which state symbol would be written after the formula of molten sodium chloride?
practiceQuestions.hint: Molten means melted. Is a melted solid dissolved in anything?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Molten sodium chloride is a pure liquid, so it is written NaCl(l). (aq) is only used when a substance is dissolved in water.

options.feedback: (aq) means dissolved in water. Molten salt has no water in it.

practiceQuestions.text: Magnesium oxide is used to line furnaces. Explain why magnesium oxide has a very high melting point.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the type of force between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions in the lattice, and how much energy it takes to overcome them.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Magnesium oxide is a giant ionic lattice. There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, acting in all directions. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these many strong forces, so the melting point is very high.

markScheme.criterion: Strong electrostatic forces / strong ionic bonds between oppositely charged ions
A lot of energy is needed to break / overcome them

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: when solid iodine is warmed and turns into a purple vapour, the I₂ molecules split apart into separate iodine atoms.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which is weaker: the I–I covalent bond inside a molecule, or the forces between neighbouring molecules?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Warming iodine only overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between the I₂ molecules. The molecules stay intact in the vapour; the strong I–I covalent bond is not broken.

practiceQuestions.text: Decide what kind of particles each substance is made of, then match it to its structure type.
practiceQuestions.hint: Metal + non-metal gives ions; a small formula of non-metals gives molecules; a network of one non-metal element is giant covalent; a pure metal is metallic.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Potassium chloride is a giant ionic lattice; oxygen exists as small O₂ molecules; diamond is a giant covalent network of carbon atoms; aluminium is a metal with a giant metallic structure.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the explanation of why brass is harder than pure copper.

metadata.blanksText: Pure copper is soft because its atoms are all the same size and sit in neat ___ that slide over one another. Mixing copper with zinc produces the alloy called ___, in which the differently sized zinc atoms ___ the regular arrangement so it can no longer slide.

practiceQuestions.hint: Picture the neat stacking of identical atoms in a pure metal, then imagine adding atoms of a different size.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pure copper has regular layers that slide. Copper mixed with zinc is brass. The zinc atoms are a different size, so they distort the layers and stop them sliding, making brass harder.

practiceQuestions.text:
The table shows some properties of two substances.

| Substance | Melting point (°C) | Conducts when solid? | Conducts when molten? |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | 98 | yes | yes |
| D | 1710 | no | no |

(a) Identify the type of structure of substance C and explain the conductivity results. (3 marks)

(b) Identify the type of structure of substance D and explain its very high melting point. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Conducting in both the solid and the liquid state is the signature of one structure type. A very high melting point with no conduction at all is the signature of another.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) C has a giant metallic structure. It contains delocalised electrons that are free to move through the structure and carry charge, whether the metal is solid or molten. (b) D is a giant covalent structure. Every atom is joined to its neighbours by many strong covalent bonds, and a very large amount of energy is needed to break them.

markScheme.criterion: C is a metal / has a giant metallic structure
Contains delocalised electrons
Electrons are free to move and carry charge in both the solid and the liquid
D is a giant covalent structure
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, needing a lot of energy
